utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We have again a late start. That's sometimes due as well to the huge flow of information and new matters that come in the morning before court. And, of course, the Judges have a busy agenda anyhow but have to deal with some of these matters, which sometimes cause us a late start. Before we invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to make a few scheduling announcements. The Chamber has reviewed the time still available under the 125 hours, and the Chamber also has reviewed what still remains of the list of witnesses. Having reviewed this, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to close its case presentation on the 16th of November, because some videolink is still scheduled for early that same week. We all know which witnesses are still on our schedule for that week to testify through videolink. The Chamber would like to invite the Defence to announce on the 8th of November, that is, the last hearing day of the week before, to inform the Chamber whether there's any intention to make a 98 bis application once the Prosecution has finished the presentation of its case. The Chamber will also take care that on the 16th of November that all the pending issues - the Chamber identified some six motions, some of a very recent date, some dating back already a little bit more - that decisions will be taken on these motions, and also that all decisions on the admission of evidence - I'm mainly thinking about exhibits on which no decision has yet been taken - that all these decisions are taken by the 16th of November. Then if there's a wish to make an oral application under Rule 98 bis, the Chamber has reserved the Tuesday, the 20th of November to hear such submissions. I earlier said that sometimes the motions on which we still have to decide came in only very recently. There is a very recent 92 bis application. Two witnesses, including protective measures. You're aware of that, Mr. Re, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I signed it, yes, so I'm -- I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one of the -- one of the questions the Chamber in that respect would have is: One of the witnesses who is now presented as a 92 bis witness also appeared on the list of witnesses that would give viva voce evidence. May we take it that the application for 92 bis supersedes this scheduling for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That -- that's the intention of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the intention. Okay, then that's clear. There's little time left. The Chamber would set a date for a response to the 92 bis application, including protective measures, by tomorrow close of business; that is, by the end of the day on the 1st of November. The Chamber is aware that it's a very short time. We're all under time pressure. That would be true for both Prosecution, Defence, and the Chamber as well. If there are no other matters, then I'd like to invite the Prosecution to call its next witness. As far as I understand, Mr. Re, the next witness will testify through a videolink, and there's no request for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct. The next witness is Mr. Qerim Kuqi, testifying via videolink from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the videolink be activated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good afternoon. Is the video and the sound -- Yes, I had forgotten to switch on my microphone. Can you hear me in Kosovo and can you see me in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the representative of the Registry in Kosovo introduce herself and tell us who are present in the room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Present in the room is Witness Kuqi, a technician, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't -- yes. Yes. Mr. Kuqi, I was informed that your sight is not very good. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true. Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will invite everyone who will appear on the screen for you to clearly introduce himself so that you know who you see. At this moment, I take it that you see the Judge in the middle of the three Judges. I'm Judge Orie. I'm the Presiding Judge. And I'm speaking at this moment to you. Mr. Kuqi, I also was informed that you cannot read. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct. I have only four years of elementary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuqi, before you give testimony before this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I will now say the words of this solemn declaration, and I would like to invite you, first of all, to stand and then to repeat my words, and I'll split it up in different portions. So therefore would you please repeat the following words: "I solemnly declare."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "That I will speak the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The whole truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "And nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuqi. Please be seated. Mr. Kuqi, you will now be first examined by Mr. Re. He will introduce himself as soon as he appears on your screen, and he's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, can you see and hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I can see you. Not very clearly, but I can. And I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. My name is David Re. I'm the Prosecutor. And I'm going to ask you some questions about your cousin Skender Kuqi. But first I'm going to ask you some details about yourself. Okay? I saw him saying something, but I didn't hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that the witness said anything. But if you would just verify with him his personal data, then we'll see how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is your name Qerim Kuqi? Were you born on the 11th of February, 1945 in Lutogllave in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you a farmer by occupation and do you still live in Lutogllave?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is Lutogllave a small village, very close to the village of Zahaq? On the road between Pec and Klina or Peja and Klina?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are there about 100 to 150 houses in Lutogllave?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your relationship to Skender Kuqi?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he born in May 1952?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know his accurate birth date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How old was he in 1998? That's when he died.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were born in 1945. How much younger than you was he approximately?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Eight or nine years older. I can't be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Skender Kuqi in 1998 live at the entrance of Lutogllave village with his family, that's his wife, Zade, and his three sons, Genc and the two other boys?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could we clarify the last -- could we clarify the answer about being younger or older. Could I ask you, Mr. Kuqi, were you older than Skender Kuqi was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was older.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you said "eight to nine years older," you meant to say that you were that many years older than Skender Kuqi. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was older.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you living in Lutogllave in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Skender Kuqi own a shop in Zahaq where he sold agricultural fertilizers?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, he had a shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he work there alone?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, but there was also someone who helped him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he a member of a political party, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was his brother, Adem, a police officer?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, he was a policeman in the former Yugoslavia, and he even now is a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1998 where was Adem working as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was unemployed for sure at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just clarify that. You said he was a police officer but unemployed at that time. What do you mean by that? When you said he's now a police officer?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was dismissed from the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you about the last time you saw Skender in 1998. Did you go to his shop?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was that in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, in July 1998 it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It was around 12.00, midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the person who helped -- helped him working in the shop there when you went there?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you speak to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did some other people come to the shop?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately how long after you got there did these other people come to the shop?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: About ten minutes it was. Less than ten minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they come on foot or by vehicle?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They came by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of car was it? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they men?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I apologise, but we've lost the video for the moment. We still have audio but don't see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will wait until the videolink has been restored. Could you inform us as soon as the video is okay again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Certainly, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will wait for another minute to see whether the videolink will be restored. If not, we'll remain stand-by but we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I inform the Trial Chamber we do have another witness -- we do have another witness in the building if the need arises, who's ready to testify. And we have a second witness by videolink who won't be available until later in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as this afternoon is concerned, we do understand that there's a second witness who will be available through videolink at 4.30. We could not start with the next witness, because we need another team of interpreters. Nevertheless, there are some not yet pending but -- well, some procedural issues in relation to the witness to appear after that. And since it will take at least another five minutes to fix the -- the videolink, the Chamber would like to hear from the parties, that is, about additional exhibits. And I do not know whether there's any problem with the 92 ter statement of the witness to come, the third witness of today. Mr. Re, no protective measures for the witness who will testify viva voce?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think so. Mr. Dutertre has the witness. As far as I know, none have been asked for as yet. And we certainly haven't put an application on. We have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, application --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Everyone is shaking their heads. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are any applications that are made after we started today, of course, the Chamber might not be aware of them. But could you check with Mr. Dutertre whether there's any reason to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're informed there's no application for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we're talking about Mr. Gojkovic, who will testify, the judge of the court in Pec. I hope that I understood all the exchanges until now, that is, that there is an application for exclusion of certain attachments to his 92 ter statements, or at least exhibits related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the position is there's no objection to be determined in relation to the text of the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There are two exhibits, the admission -- which are already on the 65 ter list and are exhibits to his 92 ter statement as to which there are objections to their admission, but that is a matter that needn't trouble the Trial Chamber at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll -- we'll see that. And then there's addition to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is pending motion for the addition of six documents in a rather different category to the list, which consist of interviews conducted by investigating judges at the Pec district court. And in respect of that, there is a motion to add those documents to the 65 ter exhibit list, and I hope that the Trial Chamber has received a written response from the Haradinaj team, I think also from the Balaj team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I've seen -- I think I have seen a response on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj to Prosecution's motion to add six relevant documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. That's filed today. I've seen that one. And I think I also have seen a Balaj ... Yes, let me just check. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And there is a correction to the motion in that the Prosecution reviewed its records and we did disclose the material on the 3rd of October in the original language. We received the translations on the 29th and disclosed them the same day. Records were -- disclosure records have been reviewed and we discovered that. We actually received them into the Office on the 14th of September, and the registration and disclosure process took until the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it, just so we're clear about this, the documents that were disclosed on the 3rd of October in their original language, untranslated, did receive a Rule 66(B) number, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We disclosed them under Rule 66(B), if that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to be clear so we're all operating on the same page with regard to what information was received when and what representations were made with regard to what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the same is true of the translations when they were served on the 29th as well, and it was sometime around 7.30 yesterday evening when the Prosecution notified the Defence with an intention to deploy these documents as part of its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything to be added to what has already been put on paper in this respect, or is there any need, Mr. Re, to respond to the opposition in the Defence filings?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's only one thing we would -- we would respond to, and that is, in our submission, the submission of the Defence has -- is legally -- is legally wrong in submitting that the documents are inadmissible, and there's a decision of the Trial Chamber on the very issue of whether statements were admissible into evidence. It was an oral ruling. I just don't have the date here. But it related to Exhibits D56, 58, and 59, and they were put in through the cross-examination of witness Rrustem Tetaj. And the Trial Chamber ruled the documents not made -- or non-ICTY statements were admissible into these proceedings. So insofar as the Defence motion, that response suggests they're not admissible, because they have to be admitted under Rule 92 bis or ter quater. That's legally incorrect and conflicts with the Trial Chamber ruling on that very issue. The Prosecution is not attempting to admit them under Rule 92 bis or quater or ter. But according to the same applicable reasoning that the Trial Chamber employed in allowing the Defence to admit into evidence Exhibits D56, 58, and 59, which were statements made to authorities other than the ICTY and not made in contemplation of legal proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the point, sorry, if I may, just in response to that -- the point that's made at paragraphs 5 and 6 of the Defence response is that the documents that the Prosecution seek here to rely upon are records of court proceedings, in the sense that they constitute interviews by investigating judges of persons in custody. And they argue to set out at paragraph 6 -- the documents that Mr. Re is referring to were the medical reports in relation to Skender Kuqi and I think one other UNMIK document. And -- and the point obviously made at paragraph 6 of the Defence response relates to records of testimony of those appearing before tribunals of national jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that the Rule 92 bis would also be the exclusive way of introducing this kind of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We -- we proceed from the premise that where the Rule makes provision for the admission of material, in those circumstances it would serve no purpose if -- indeed, the Rule would be unnecessary, if there were no otherwise exclusionary principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This same approach has not been taken in relation to police statements given at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In -- sorry, in the course of these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The same approach has been taken, so far as the Defence is concerned, in relation to the admission of that material, I think, but the Trial Chamber has ruled certain of that material to be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm not saying what your position was but... Let us see. We can't start with the -- neither of the two remaining witnesses. Could we be informed about how much time it would still take to re-establish the videolink in ... Yes, I do understand that the videolink functions well again. I therefore seek this to be confirmed by the representative of the Registrar in Kosovo. Can you see us? Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. We have been reconnected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, let's just go back to where we were before the videolink broke. I was asking you about the people who came in the car. You said there were two of them. My next question: Were -- were they men?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they dressed in? Civilian clothes or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: In -- they were wearing jackets and they were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of jackets?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Like military-like jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe them a little bit better?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I can't describe them any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they coloured?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They -- they were masked, and there was black and there was some red colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Re, I understood - but it could be that I wrongly understood - the answer to your question "What sort of jackets," the first word to be a reference to the colour rather than the word "like." This will be checked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you saw some black and red. Are you referring to the jackets?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. No, no. They were wearing masks, and you couldn't see -- distinguish who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was the black --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: The mask was red and black.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did they do when they came to the shop?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: When they entered the shop, they shouted in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of accent did they have when they spoke in -- shouted in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They spoke very well Serbian, because I -- I speak Serbian. I understand Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, did they have any sort of Serbian accent? From their accent, where did it appear that they had come from?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I think they were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you think they were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I think they were Serbs. I think they were Serbs, because -- because they only spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did they shout?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: "Hands up. Get out."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They were armed with automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: What kind? I was so worried that I didn't see well what -- what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did they do with you and what did they do with Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They shouted at him. They took him out to the garage, where they kept the goods. I remained inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did either of the men remain with you when you remained inside?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: There was only my uncle, who was, like, 10 metres away from the door. And at the time they searched -- they searched my pockets to see if I had anything in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said "uncle." Are you referring to your cousin Skender by saying "uncle," or was there another person there?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. No, there was no other person once Skender was taken away. There was no other in the room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: There was -- we misheard the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is "uncle" and "cousin" the same in the translation is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. He may have said "dalje" [phoen], but it was heard as "daje," which is the word for "uncle."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The further clarification is that only that person was in the room, I think, would do Mr. Re. Was there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the Chamber is satisfied that only Skender was there, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what the witness said. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said they searched your pockets to see if you had anything in them. What did they do with their weapons when they were speaking to you and speaking to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They had pointed them to my head and urged me not to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long were the men there for?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They stayed for two, three minutes. No more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said they took your cousin Skender to the garage. Did you see what they did with him in the garage?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. No, I -- I couldn't see, because the door was closed and I was inside the room, so I couldn't see what they were doing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They took him in a car, and I don't know where they took him to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask if you saw or observed that taking him in a car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that they left together in a car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to know how do you know that? My name is Frank Hoepfel, by the way. I am also a Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. You saw that they left together in a car. And can you tell us what happened in between, before the car left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know. I don't know what to say, because they were talking at a place away from where I was. They were inside the garage, and I couldn't hear or see them in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And was the car in the garage, or how happened it then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The car was in the garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said they arrived in a car and they left in a car. How many cars were there?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They came in one car and there was Skender's car in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they leave in their car or Skender's car or both cars?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which car was Skender in?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: His own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he driving?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there were two men. Were they in their car or was one of them in Skender's car?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: One was in Skender's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did the two cars go? By that I mean in which direction.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: The direction of Kline.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were the two --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It was Kline, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And were the two cars traveling together in the direction of Klina?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you could see, did Skender go voluntarily with these two armed men wearing military-like jackets and masks on their faces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Are you sure this is a question which would lead to some result? Can you tell from -- by looking if somebody does something voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not going to answer that in front of the -- in front of the witness, with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said you saw two armed men wearing military-like jackets, automatic weapons, masks on their faces. They came into the shop, put a gun in your face, said, "Hands up," took Skender to the garage, then they drove off with Skender. As far as you see, from what you saw, did Skender go voluntarily - that's of his own free will - with them?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a voluntary departure or not. I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could we give it another try to find the colour of the jacket. Mr. Kuqi, you said these were military-like jackets. Could you tell us what the colour of the jackets was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say the colour, but it was like camouflage. Like the rest of the army have similar jackets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And camouflage we find in different colours again. I've seen greenish, I've seen brownish, I've seen bluish camouflage uniforms. Could you tell us which or perhaps a combination of these colours this was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't -- I don't know what to say, but they were camouflage jackets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these two men had any patches or insignia on their jackets or masks?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. They had no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, where were the KLA stationed in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: They were stationed in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know whether they were stationed in Jablanica at the time?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the KLA in your village at the time when Skender left with these men?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were KLA members there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were the nearest Serbian forces - by that I mean the Serbian police and military - to your village at the time?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know accurately, but I know that the police station is not further than 5 or 6 kilometres away. It was the area occupied by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a KLA staff or headquarters in your village at the time Skender was taken away or left with the men?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone what had happened to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I told Skender's brother of what happened. I told it to Adem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he do about it?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He asked me who they were, and I said to him that they spoke Serbian, so they may be Serbian. This is what I told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know about any relatives of Skender going to KLA HQ, or headquarters, in Jablanica to find out what happened to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I know only what his brother told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did his brother tell you?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He told me that Skender is dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell you what inquiries he and other members of the family had made to find out what had happened to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know who went where.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Abdulla Kuqi and Amrush Kuqi? What did they do to find out what happened to Skender?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Adem went to ask about the fate of his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who did he go to ask?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know where he went. I don't know whom he asked or where he went. I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you find out -- sorry, how long after Skender left with the two men did you find out that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, but I only know that his brother was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Was it within days or weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It was within weeks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you told how he had died?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Skender's brothers, Sokol Kuqi or Adem Kuqi tell you who they thought were the men who Skender left with, that is, whether they were Albanians or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Skender was, apart from owning the shop, was a teacher?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember well. Probably he was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of car did Skender have, the one that was in the garage and the one he left in?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It was a Mercedes. I don't recall its colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you tell us about Skender's health condition? You said he was running a shop. What was his general health condition like in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: To my recollection, he was in a good health condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember him ever -- ever making complaints about illnesses around that time?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: No. No, no, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how often did you see him generally and in the period leading up to when you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Whenever I wanted to buy something in his store, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, how often was that?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I can't say. Not very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just to conclude, was that the last time you ever saw Skender, the time you saw him leave with those men in his car in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson, I do understand from your nodding that there's no need to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith? Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No need either, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, since Defence counsel have no questions for you and since the Bench has no questions for you either, this concludes your testimony before the -- this Chamber of the Tribunal. I'd like to thank you very much that you came and that you've answered all questions put to you, and I hope that you will have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then although the videolink should remain on stand-by, we can disconnect at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For logistical and practical purposes, the Chamber understands that it does not make any sense at this moment to start with the third witness scheduled for today and then to interrupt that again for the videolink, so therefore, unless the parties have any useful other suggestion, we'll have a relatively long break. We might come back a bit early, before the videolink can start, so as to -- perhaps if we are already at the point to deliver any decisions on the six exhibits to be added to the exhibit list or if there's any other matter the Chamber would have to consider during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. -- I was looking at Mr. Re at this moment. Mr. Re, is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's just that we have some possible concerns about scheduling and time. We have another witness scheduled to come tomorrow. I think it's Witness 37. Judge Gojkovic, Mr. Dutertre says he'll be about half an hour in examination-in-chief with him. And we understand the witness is actually -- the other witness for the videolink is actually traveling and hasn't reached the office yet and is estimated to be here by 4.30 but there's no guarantee that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is interpreters teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I understand to be the problem. We can't switch from teams every half an hour. That -- if that can be resolved, of course the Chamber will have no problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They're waving, Your Honour. They're waving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there's some communication. If you would -- Are there no problems as far as interpreter teams are concerned? I'm listening to the English Channel, but I can -- If you could point at what channel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're supposed to work until 7.00. Anyway, the team is ready to work until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- if that is the case ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to have been a miscommunication as far as problem with changing interpreters teams is concerned. The Chamber then suggests that we have a break for 25 minutes; that -- then, Mr. Dutertre, you said half an hour. I'm looking at you and you're not nodding "yes" but you're nodding very strongly "yes." Then we could start examination-in-chief of that witness then switch to the videolink to Kosovo again and start cross-examination after the break. The Chamber during this break now will also further consider the issue of the six exhibits to be added, and, of course, admission of those exhibits is -- although a separate matter, is linked to it. We'll also consider whether we do it in once or whether we split it up. And we also consider whether we'll do it on a provisional basis or whether we'll give decisions right away, firm decisions. If it would be provisional decisions then as we have done before, then, of course, an opportunity -- and further opportunity will be given to make submissions on the matter. We'll have a break until -- Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that specific issue. Because the documents were identified as 66(B) documents, I think it might be of some importance for the Chamber to know whether or not there was an informal translation of those documents or some other form of translation of those documents that the Prosecution had within its own possession, custody, and control which allowed them to define the documents in that fashion, because we had no knowledge at all whatsoever apart from the designation of the Rule and the documents in a language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- untranslated until the very late day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me understand. If the Office of the Prosecution receives documents, of course they would not know what's in those documents, so they'll ask for a translation to be made in order to identify --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But often --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the importance of the -- so, therefore, the question whether there was already a provisional translation available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oftentimes, the Prosecution, I believe, there's been representations made during this trial, the Prosecution gets an informal understanding of what the documents may be or an informal translation so they have some idea what the import or the relevance of those documents are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, do I -- is it you or Mr. Dutertre who could answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information I have is that I think we received almost 70 pages -- we had someone read through them and they prepared one or two lines on those which were potentially relevant and then we had them translated. That was -- we only received the translation on the 29th, which is two days -- two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You had not made up your mind at that moment whether or not to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, we -- we didn't make up our mind till we received the translations and read the full documents on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that your information about the content was minimal at the time, limited to just a couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the avoidance of doubt, on behalf of the Brahimaj team, we do join -- we have not made a formal written opposition, but we -- we are particularly concerned by the page -- what appears as page 51 of the proposed additional documents, which is a -- a wildly speculative hearsay-upon-hearsay reference to Jabllanice, and to that extent we would wish to add that to the table of objections already filed by our colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. We have a break until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, will it be you who will examine the next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then an application was made for protective measures, and we have not yet received responses from the Defence. Mr. Emmerson. But first we have to go into -- are we in private session at this moment? We should be in private session. And, of course, the picture of the videolink was not shown to the public, I take it, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it wasn't. And we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. For the next witness to be called, there was an application for protective measures: Pseudonym, voice distortion, and face distortion. The application was not opposed by Defence. The Chamber grants the protective measures, although several grounds were supporting the request that the Chamber limits itself at this moment to establishing that the witness and/or his family members are still living in Kosovo, that the anticipated testimony may antagonise persons in an unstable situation in Kosovo, as agreed upon by the parties. These are the reasons, not to say that the other reasons would not be valid, but these reasons in itself justify the granting of protective measures. We then return in -- no, we stay in open -- Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: [Microphone not activated] I'd like to introduce his evidence, if I may, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would like to start in private session. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we turn in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to think about your last -- your -- your late brother and when you last saw him in 1998. Can you remember the time --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the time of year that you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. I don't want to lie to you, sir. I don't want to lie. I don't know the exact time. Without being 100 per cent sure, I don't want to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thanks for that. But can you tell us perhaps the season that you last saw him in? Was it, for example, summer or -- or autumn? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It's an approximate time that I will give you. I think it was summer-time. I'm not -- not summer, but spring. Approximately. I am not sure. I don't want to lie to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I think we're having a little trouble with transcription. I think that the audibility of -- of the translation is not very good. I'm certainly having to resort to the written word, and I gather that that's causing problems for our ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any problems at this moment? Yes, there are? Could it -- could it be resolved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the problems have been resolved. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honours for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. You're not sure, but you think it might have been spring. Okay. And where -- where was your late brother --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I'm not certain. I don't want to lie to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Thank you. Where was your late brother living when you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: His house was in the same village with me. His wife was from (redacted) and her father was elderly and ill, so his wife went to live with his -- with her father to take care of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks for that. Thanks for that information. How -- how old was your brother? Your late brother.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: After me. He was younger than me. But I think it was two or -- he was two or three years younger than me. I am not very sure. I can show you my identity card for you to see how old I am. And that would deduce his age.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that's necessary. I think we can get -- get an idea. Thank you very much. Anyway, he was about -- he was only about two or three youngers -- years younger than you. Can you tell us something about his physical condition? Did -- just wait for my question. What -- what I'd like -- what I'd like to know -- just wait --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 71, would you please listen to me for a second. Wait until Mr. Di Fazio has formulated his question. Just wait until he invites you to answer the question so that you don't miss anything, and it will certainly save time if you wait and listen well. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Okay. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'd -- what I'd like to know is about your brother -- your brother's physical condition. Did he have all his fingers?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was -- he had only one finger in one hand because of an accident with a bomb. When it was the first war he found a bomb, a grenade, and that exploded and cut off his fingers. But he was -- he was never in the army. He didn't go to school either, because he became handicapped, and he received social assistance. He was disabled. He was sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks. And your brother had suffered that disability years -- years before, I understand. Is that right? Years before 1998.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: When he was at the age to go to school, he didn't go to school because he was diagnosed as disabled. How can I tell it to you? How can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's fine. And thank you for explaining all of that. And did he get a pension for -- for being -- for being disabled?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, he received economic assistance, social assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: The entire town of Gjakova knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He was disabled, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And he was getting that pension for disability in 1998 as well?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know, but before that, yes. During the Communist regime he -- he received that assistance because of that problem he has. I don't know how much he received, but he did receive an allowance for being disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, I want you to think back to the period of time soon after your brother disappeared. Sorry, the -- let me rephrase that. Soon after the period of time you last saw your brother. In that time, did you see a gentleman named Shkelzen Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Once only. They -- they told me it was Shkelzen, because I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Just wait and let me ask you the -- just wait. Don't speak. And let me ask you the questions. Okay? So that we can get through this quickly. All right? I want you to tell the Judges who are listening here about how it is that you came to see this man Shkelzen Haradinaj and where you saw him and how you got to see him. So can you -- can you tell us that, please. How was it that you came to be in the company of Shkelzen Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: In Gllogjan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So how did you get from wherever you were to Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He asked me, "Do you smoke?" I said, "Yes." And then he said, "Do you have cigarettes with you?" I said, "No," and then he gave me two cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no, just --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: He asked one of the boys who were there, "Give him some tobacco."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just listen to my question. Before you saw Shkelzen Haradinaj and before you went to Glodjane, were you living at your house?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Were you taken from your house --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. At the time that you -- you saw Shkelzen Haradinaj or just before that occasion, were you living at your house -- at your house, at your home? Were you just living at home?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was living at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: And I went there from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Great. Thank you. Now, what I'd like you to do is to tell the Judges how you got from your home to Glodjane. How did you -- how was that accomplished? How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: How did I go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: By what means you are asking me or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. How did you get there? Did you go in a car or did you -- someone take you? Did you go on a bicycle? How was it done?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I went there by car. By car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you go there? How did you come to be going -- leaving your house to go to Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: We had a problem. They asked about a young man, who he was. And I said -- where he was. I said, "He is not here." They said, "Come with us to Gllogjan." And they asked me where he was, and I said again, "No, I don't know where he is." And then they asked me if I smoked, and they gave me those two cigarettes, and as I said to you earlier, I returned home after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd just like to ask you a few more questions about this. You say "they." Who -- who was -- who came to your house and asked you these things? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Those who came to my house, they came from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the persons who came to my house?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am. I'd like to know some things about them and I'd like to know what you can tell us about these -- these people. First -- okay?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, these people told me to go with them and to tell them where that's -- that young boy was. I went with them and I replied that I didn't know where that young man was. I took these two cigarettes that I mentioned and I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And these -- these men who came from the headquarters, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they were the ones who took you from your house to the Glodjane headquarters.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And who was -- you don't have to mention names, but can you just tell us about the young boy that you've been telling us about, who they were asking you about. Who did you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Where I went? There?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, look -- MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps, if Your Honours please, we could go into private session for a moment it might be advisable, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've only told us part of the story, and we want to hear all of the story. You've told us that some KLA men came and they were from Glodjane and they took you there. And now we want to know what happened once you arrived there. We want you to tell the story --

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- of what happened when you arrived at the headquarters in Glodjane. Can you tell us who -- who you saw there?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: Nothing happened. They asked me there, "Where is he?" I said, "I don't know." They asked me whether I smoked, and I said, "Yes." "Do you have cigarettes?" I said, "No." They gave me two packets of cigarettes. And they said, "Do you want us to drive you home, to take you home, or are you going home on yourself -- by yourself?" And I said, "I'm going there by myself." And that's how I came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've already told us that you -- you -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I think moments ago you said that Shkelzen Haradinaj was at Glodjane. I don't want to misquote you, but I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- if perhaps you check the transcript, I think the witness said "I was told."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I didn't know him. Later on I learned that it was Shkelzen and he -- he was -- he was a very nice man, and he even offered me cigarettes and gave me two packets to take with me. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I see. So -- okay. Well -- thank you. So later you learned that the man who gave you cigarettes was Shkelzen Haradinaj and he was a very kind man. Okay.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: It was after that that I asked other people. I said, "Who is that man?" And they told me, "He is Shkelzen Haradinaj." I'd never heard of him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And did -- was the young boy the only topic of conversation, or did you speak about something else as well?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, because time has passed and I can't remember things that happened three days ago, but the only thing I will tell you, that we got along very well and we had no problem and they gave me those cigarettes. We -- we had a good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how long had your late brother -- how long had your late brother been missing by the time you had this encounter with Mr. Shkelzen Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: I did not know when he had disappeared, when he had gone to Gllogjan; I did not know that he had disappeared, I did not know that yet. After the war had ended, I heard from people… I did not know at all, I thought he was alive; I did not know whether he had disappeared or not, I only heard from people what they said, I did not know for sure. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please. And would you just wait a moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: QERIM KUQI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd just like you to have a look at a -- at a -- at a video. And look and listen as carefully as you can to this particular video that's going to be played to you. And the -- the -- it's an excerpt, if Your Honours please, and it's referred to as 65 ter 2125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I think it will eventually. Yes, it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P1192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any -- MR. DI FAZIO: And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any words spoken on the video? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. And I think that you should have a -- a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, more important is that the booth have the transcript. Of course, the Chamber always would like to have it as well. But if it's in English on the screen, then ... Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Do Your Honours have the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think we have it. But let's -- MR. DI FAZIO: All right. We'll proceed. Thank you. Just -- would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, this is an excerpt from another exhibit in the case. You'll be informed of that number shortly. Secondly, it should be in private session, because it will depict the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 71, I would like to thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal, although you remained in Kosovo, and for having answered the questions that were put to you. We wish you the best with your health and we hope that you'll be back home in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my best regards to everyone present. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May God give you a long life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Witness 71. We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bye-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we can disconnect the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had a -- first of all, we are in open session. I think we can pull the curtains up again. The curtains were down in order to disenable anyone to look at the screens in the courtroom. It was not closed session. We did cut the pause rather short beyond for what is usually acceptable for the interpreters and the technicians. Now, we could do two things: Either to -- at this moment to have an additional break of ten minutes and then to continue, or to continue right away and to stop ten minutes earlier. I would have a slight preference for the latter solution, if the technicians in the booth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So do the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since Mr. Dutertre promised us that he would not need more than 30 minutes, I would like to enquire with the Defence how much time as matters stand now would be needed for cross-examination. I'm not suggesting that we could finish for the day, not at all. It even makes it easier to stop ten minutes early if there is no chance that we'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is no chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would have thought somewhat in the region of an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. So we could start cross-examination today and then would -- we'd finish for the day at ten minutes to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you need any further indication? It would be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, most --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- most important for me was that by stopping at ten minutes to 7.00, that we would not miss a chance to -- to conclude the testimony of the next witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber is interested to know how much time, but we'll hear that from you at a later stage. Mr. Dutertre, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For one reason or another the interpreters cannot hear you, Mr. Dutertre. Would you please repeat what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Is there a decision regarding the six documents that we wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a partial decision. Good cause has been shown to add them to the list, which doesn't say anything about whether these are exhibits that are admissible. The Chamber would have to look at them in quite some detail to see what the merits are in the Defence submissions. You didn't make it that easy for us, Mr. Dutertre, because when we tried to decipher what was in front of us, we noticed that you sometimes attach the English translation of another statement to one statement of Mr. Re and then we find the translation of -- after some research, seems to be the translation of the statement of a witness B. We have not had sufficient time to go through it in sufficient detail to finally make up our mind as to whether they could be admitted, yes or no, but the Chamber does not at this moment object that these exhibits would be marked for identification, and, of course, some formal questions as to, Do you recognise this report, Was it you who took the statement? These, of course, might be relevant, these -- such questions might be relevant at this moment, but nothing as of yet has been said, as far as admission into evidence, and what weight, if any at all, should be given to the content of it. Then we wait until the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I apologise for the translation problems, for the wrong translation being attached to the document. The Defence had already voiced some objections as to the annexes that were attached to the testimony of -- or the statement. This had to do with two annexes. And we had moved along, which was to maintain our wish to have them tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's about what happened to the medical people who went for -- I think for health care for the children -- preventive health care for the children. Mr. Dutertre, there seems to be also a newspaper article. Does that add anything to -- to the other sources? Do you think this more ...? We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher will now hand out to you the text of that declaration, and I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojkovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think I have to explain to you court proceedings, Mr. Gojkovic. You'll first be examined by Mr. Dutertre, counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to present the 92 ter witness statement, and we have a binder that has been prepared for that purpose. And Madam Usher can now give it to the witness, but it is already the 65 ter exhibit number 2102, which I'd like to have displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without further ado, I can already ask the witness to refer to his binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, would you mind taking the binder in order to look at the exhibit number which is the 92 ter witness statement. You have the text in Serbian and in English. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you look at your screen. Most likely you'll find it on your screen as well. Madam Usher, is the ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Judge, I have two questions regarding this document which is put to you by Madam Usher. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, may I ask you the following: With full respect for the function of this witness in his domestic jurisdiction, I think it might be confusing if we have on the record -- if you were addressed by "Your Honour" or by "Judge." That's not in any way to not fully respect your position in your jurisdiction, but in, of course, in this courtroom, Mr. Gojkovic, as -- if anyone would understand this, it would be you, I take it, that you are Mr. Gojkovic, who is a witness in this case. Mr. Dutertre, would you please address, again with full respect for the function, the position held by Mr. Gojkovic, would you please do that in order to avoid confusion on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, do you remember signing the document you have in front of you and which is displayed on the screen on the 23rd of October, 2007?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that I signed that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Does this represent the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that I said in the document is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last thing. Were the questions that were put to you during this interview, the said interview on the 23rd of October, to be asked again of you today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely I would give the same answers. I would answer the same way. Just this, if I may add. If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us, would you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are certain vague statements or assertions in the statement, but as a whole they do not change the content of the key facts that are contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless Mr. Gojkovic wants to add anything, I would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything at this moment you'd like to add, please do so, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add now, but if there are any questions, I am prepared, if I can, of course, to answer them, in view of the time that has passed since then. It's been eight years since the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said whatever you found in the statement is -- is -- is the truth, and the statement reflects -- the written version of the statement reflects what you said in your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Considering the -- the extensive experience the gentleman has had in the law, for him to make a comment that there are certain vague statements or assertions in the statement, I have some concern with regard to whether or not as he has reviewed his statement he believes there should be some corrections or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I asked him whether he would have to add something. And if something is vague usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What precision there is, the more need there might be for questions. If there is any matter, I think you can deal with that in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm raising it now is I don't want to get in this position that we've gotten in with other witnesses when we have actually been discussing their statements with them and they have indicated that they were not aware of something that they had actually signed or in some other fashion had not been so attentive to the statement. We could not rely upon it. Since the 92 ter statement does take the position of being testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The OTP has already -- has also prepared an index, a summary of the annex. This is 65 number 2134. I would like to seek that document into evidence as well. And I wish to get exhibit numbers for the annexes mentioned therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections against the 92 ter statement? Then that is admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar will prepare MFI numbers for the annexes and, of course, within the limits the Chamber set before. Then, Mr. Dutertre -- Mr. Dutertre, usually the beginning of -- the beginning of an examination of a witness is to establish his personal data. I don't think that that has happened yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm coming to this. One moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, can you please state your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 7th of August, 1948 in the village of Crni Vrh near Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb, a citizen of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1998 I was elected as the president of the Pec District Court, and I am still at that post today, but the headquarters or the seat of the district court office has been relocated to Ljeskovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, this is in the 92 ter statement, isn't it? Which is in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, I do have a 92 ter statement summary, if you think it is opportune to read it this -- to read it now at this stage of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you explained to Mr. Gojkovic what -- what the function of this is? Mr. Gojkovic, for the public character of this trial, if someone -- if a written statement is introduced into evidence, then the public, of course, misses what the evidence is, and therefore a summary is then read so that the public is aware of it. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
